content:
A popular explanation of conversion to Islam has one word in it: marriage. People are said to become Muslim to marry a Muslim, and for no other reason. The converts themselves, when asked, tell a different story.

In its 2017 survey of American Muslims, Pew Research Center found that 21% had converted to Islam, and it asked them, in their own words, why. Their answers fell into seven groups, and marriage was one of the smaller ones.[1]

This article aims to provide context to the question, insha'Allah, in the seven reasons converts gave, set beside the Quran's own account of how people come to faith. The Quran names the choice as free: "Let there be no compulsion in religion: Truth stands out clear from Error" (2:256).[2]

The largest group, about one in four (24%), said they preferred the beliefs and teachings of Islam, or found more meaning in it than in their previous faith.[1]

The centre of those teachings is the oneness of God, given in a surah of four verses: "Say: He is Allah, the One and Only; Allah, the Eternal, Absolute; He begetteth not, nor is He begotten; And there is none like unto Him" (112:1 to 4).[2] Pew found that about half of American converts had been Protestants before, and one in five Catholics.[1]

About one in five said that reading religious texts and studying the faith were the main reasons.[1] The Quran asks for exactly this: "Do they not then earnestly seek to understand the Qur'an, or are their hearts locked up by them?" (47:24).[2]

Iulian Vamanu and Elysia Guzik have studied what reading means in recent conversion narratives in both Christianity and Islam.[3] We set out the questions such readers meet in from atheism to Islam: 5 questions.

One in ten (10%) said they wanted to belong to a community.[1] The Quran describes the believers as a single brotherhood (49:10), and the five daily prayers, the Friday prayer and Ramadan put that belonging into practice.

Thomas Sealy's study of British converts examines continuity as well as change in their religious identity.[4]

9% said a friend or a public leader introduced them to the faith.[1] The Quran tells Muslims how to make that introduction: "Invite (all) to the Way of thy Lord with wisdom and beautiful preaching; and argue with them in ways that are best and most gracious" (16:125).[2]

An introduction opens a door. The Quran is plain that the decision is God's guidance and the person's choice: "It is true thou wilt not be able to guide every one, whom thou lovest; but Allah guides those whom He will" (28:56).[2]

9% named marriage, the same share as those introduced by a friend.[1]

Islamic law looks at the intention behind every act. The first hadith in al-Bukhari's collection begins: "The reward of deeds depends upon the intentions and every person will get the reward according to what he has intended." It names marriage itself: "whoever emigrated for worldly benefits or for a woman to marry, his emigration was for what he emigrated for."[5] A conversion is weighed before God by the intention behind it.

8% gave other family reasons.[1] Pew does not divide this group further.

The Quran keeps the duty to parents in place even when faith divides them: "bear them company in this life with justice (and consideration)" (31:15).[2] We set out the stories of converts and their families in 4 Indonesian conversion stories.

Another 8% said they were exploring their own spirituality.[1] The Quran describes that search as a return to the human pattern: "the pattern on which He has made mankind ... that is the standard Religion" (30:30), and names where it ends: "for without doubt in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find satisfaction" (13:28).[2]

Karin van Nieuwkerk's study of Dutch converts reads conversion through biography and choice, the life that leads to the decision.[6]

The bottom line

American converts gave seven reasons for becoming Muslim, and the largest was a preference for Islam's beliefs and teachings, followed by reading and study. Community, an introduction by a friend, marriage, family and a personal spiritual search follow, each named by one in ten or fewer. The claim that conversion is mostly about marriage does not survive the converts' own answers.

The numbers also need their limits stated. Pew's 2025 study of 36 countries found that in the 13 it could analyse for Islam, 3% or fewer of adults had entered or left it.[7] Conversion is a personal decision, rare in any country, and the Quran leaves it where it belongs: "Let him who will believe, and let him who will, reject (it)" (18:29).[2] Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Pew Research Center, "U.S. Muslims Concerned About Their Place in Society, but Continue to Believe in the American Dream", chapter 6, "Religious Beliefs and Practices", 26 July 2017.
  2. Quran 2:256; 13:28; 16:125; 18:29; 28:56; 30:30; 31:15; 47:24; 49:10; 112:1 to 4, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Iulian Vamanu and Elysia Guzik, "'Closer to God': Meanings of Reading in Recent Conversion Narratives within Christianity and Islam", Journal of Religious & Theological Information 14, nos. 3–4 (2015), pp. 63–78.
  4. Thomas Sealy, "British Converts to Islam: Continuity, Change, and Religiosity in Religious Identity", Journal of Contemporary Religion 36, no. 3 (2021), pp. 421–439.
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Revelation, the report of Umar ibn al-Khattab on intentions.
  6. Karin van Nieuwkerk, "Biography and Choice: Female Converts to Islam in the Netherlands", Islam and Christian–Muslim Relations 19, no. 4 (2008), pp. 431–447.
  7. Kirsten Lesage, Kelsey Jo Starr and William Miner, "Religious Switching Into and Out of Islam", in Around the World, Many People Are Leaving Their Childhood Religions, Pew Research Center, 26 March 2025.
